title: Flock: A Knowledge Graph Foundation Model via Learning on Random Walks
one_liner: Flock breaks symmetries in knowledge graphs by adding structured randomness while keeping equivariance in distribution, so it can tell apart relations that look the same but mean different things.
lead: Knowledge graphs are databases of facts (like 'Einstein authored relativity') stored as edges between entities. When a model learns from one graph, it should work on new graphs with the same structure. The problem: enforcing perfect symmetry (equivariance) makes the model blind to relations that look structurally similar but are semantically distinct. Flock adds controlled randomness to break ties while preserving equivariance in the aggregate, making it the first universal approximator for this task.

paras: A knowledge graph is just a list of triples: 'Einstein, authored, relativity'. When you have a model trained on one graph, you want it to work on a new graph with unknown entities and new relations. The trick is to teach it the structural patterns so it can generalize.

Current methods enforce equivariance — a fancy word for: if you swap two entities that have the same role, the model's answer swaps the same way. This helps generalization because it teaches the model to rely on structure rather than memorizing specific entities. But it has a fatal flaw: if two relations look the same structurally (same pattern of who connects to whom), the model treats them as identical even if they mean completely different things. A classic example: 'authored' and 'co-authored' might have the same structure but very different meanings. The model cannot tell them apart.

callout.html: Flock adds random noise to break symmetries at inference time, while the aggregated predictions (averaged over many samples) preserve the symmetric property, so the model learns to distinguish relations that look identical but mean different things because the randomness forces it to notice subtle structural differences.

panels.title: 1. Two structurally identical relations

panels.title: 2. Deterministic equivariance treats them as one

panels.caption: Perfect symmetry makes the model blind to semantic difference.

panels.title: 3. Flock adds structured randomness to each walk
panels.caption: Random sampling breaks ties without losing the structure.

panels.title: 4. Aggregate behavior stays equivariant

steps.text: For each entity, take a random path through the graph edges.
Turn the path into a list of entity names, one after another.
Pass the sequence through a transformer (a sequence-reading model).
Combine predictions from many random walks via learned weights.
Use aggregated representation to guess missing entity-relation pairs.

object.h2: The move: add randomness to the sampling, not the learning
paras: Flock does not add randomness to the model weights or the loss function. Instead, it adds randomness to the input: each time the model sees an entity, it samples a different random walk (a different path through the graph neighbors). This structured randomness at inference time breaks symmetries — two structurally identical relations get represented differently because they are sampled differently — while the aggregated answer (the average over all samples) stays deterministic and equivariant: swapping interchangeable entities produces the same average answer.

hidden.name: Aggregate symmetry across samples
paras: Distributional equivariance means: if you swap two interchangeable entities in the input graph, the distribution over the model's outputs stays the same, but individual samples can differ. It is like saying: if you shuffle a deck and draw one card, you might get a different card, but the average value of the card over many shuffles stays the same.

Flock measures this by enforcing that the pooled (aggregated) representation respects symmetry, even though each individual random walk breaks it. The paper proves Flock is a universal approximator — meaning it can learn any function that respects this distributional symmetry.

heat.caption: Darker means stronger signal for a relation. Individual samples vary (noise breaks ties); the average is stable (equivariance in distribution).

reads.html: When you sample many random walks and average their predictions, the result is symmetric — swapping structurally similar entities gives the same average prediction. But each walk is different, so the model can learn what makes 'authored' different from 'co-authored' because the pooling weights learn to emphasize different walks for different relations, and different walks yield different sequences that the transformer can distinguish.

Flock respects probabilistic node-relation equivariance: the joint distribution over node and relation representations is invariant to permutations that preserve graph structure, enabling universality while breaking deterministic equivariance.

mechanism.h2: Why adding randomness at inference preserves learning
paras: Randomness in the input (which walk you sample) does not touch the learning rule. The learning rule aggregates (pools) predictions from many walks using learned weights, and the aggregation respects symmetry. This means the model learns a single, symmetric function of the graph structure, but the intermediate steps (each walk) are noisy and can be different.

Why does this break semantic symmetries? When two relations are structurally identical but the walks happen to reach different neighbors first, the sequence model sees different input sequences. The learned weights during pooling can then learn to weight one walk higher when the relation is 'authored' and another walk higher when it is 'co-authored', because the pooling weights are relation-specific. The randomness forces the model to use the subtle structural differences (which neighborhoods are reached, in which order) as signals for semantic meaning.

stages.s: Encode path as sequence, convert to list of numbers via transformer
Sample second walk, convert to numbers again
Average the number-lists with learned importance weights

math.words: Relation prediction is the average prediction from each sampled walk, weighted by learned importance scores. The weight for each walk depends on the entity pair and relation.
math.equation: pred_rel = sum_walks w_walk * embedding_walk / sum_walks w_walk
symbols: Predicted probability of the relation (number between 0 and 1)
Learned importance weight for this particular walk and relation
The vector produced by embedding this random walk with a transformer

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Relation 'authored': Entity pair (Einstein, relativity). Sample 3 random walks.
Walk 1 path (Einstein -> co-worker -> relativity): weight 0.1, score from model 0.9.
Walk 2 path (Einstein -> wrote -> relativity): weight 0.7, score from model 0.95.
Walk 3 path (Einstein -> studied -> relativity): weight 0.2, score from model 0.8.
The model learns to give walk 2 high weight for 'authored' because that walk sees the direct wrote connection; other walks get lower weight for this relation.

math.note: The learned weights are the key: they let the model ignore irrelevant walks and emphasize the walks that reveal the true relation, even when the overall graph structure looks symmetric.

charts.title: Old methods (deterministic equivariance)
charts.note: Methods collapse structurally similar relations, failing on semantic distinctions.

charts.title: Flock (probabilistic equivariance)
charts.note: Randomness in sampling lets Flock distinguish relations that deterministic methods conflate.

items.b: Too much randomness, too few samples.
items.html: If you sample only one or two walks, the randomness dominates and the model learns noise instead of structure. You need enough samples for the law of large numbers to kick in; the aggregate has to be stable.

items.b: Learned weights can overfit to training relations.
items.html: The pooling weights learn which walks matter for each relation. On a new graph with new relations, those weights may not transfer, especially if the new relations have different structural signatures.

Sampling random walks and converting each one into a list of numbers with a transformer is expensive. On huge knowledge graphs with billions of edges, inference time grows with the number of samples because you have to do this conversion many times.

items.b: Done right: Flock balances number of samples.
items.html: The paper tunes the sample count so that randomness is enough to break ties but not so much that it drowns out signal. This is dataset-dependent.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Build a mini knowledge graph with two relations that are structurally identical (same in-degree, out-degree, same neighbor types) but semantically distinct: for example, 'parent-of' and 'aunt-of' in a family tree, or 'produced-by' and 'co-produced-by' in a music dataset. Train Flock on this graph, leaving out a few edges. Measure whether the model correctly predicts which relation is missing.
demo.closing: The demo must show that Flock's accuracy on semantically distinct but structurally identical relations is at least 30-40 percentage points higher than a deterministic equivariance baseline. This proves the randomness actually breaks the symmetry.
